speaker: Tom Mueller
title: Impulse Space CEO Tom Mueller - Propulsion, and Rocket Engines - NSF Live
question: In orbital launch vehicles, do you actually need a low-thrust upper-stage engine to insert payloads into orbit accurately without overshooting?
guest: No. We used to worry about that a lot with Merlin Vacuum because it is a gigantic last-stage engine—around 220,000 pounds of thrust—and it inserts accurately. It is really about understanding your cutoff impulse. When you give the engine the kill signal to shut off, you need to know how much propellant is still in there and burning, and how much cutoff impulse you have, so you can time it perfectly and hit the target. It is certainly going to be harder to hit the bullseye than an RL10 or something with 20,000 pounds—a tenth of the thrust. On our stage we are down at 15,000 pounds, with less than a tenth of the propellant on board, and we can throttle deeply if we really want to hit it close. If somebody needs us to hit within a tiny fraction of a percent, we can always throttle way down and do that. I am not too worried about it; I think we can hit that cutoff impulse really accurately.

models.answer:
No, low thrust isn't strictly required, but it helps, and what really matters is how precisely you can control the total impulse delivered at shutdown.

Insertion accuracy depends on the guidance system commanding engine cutoff at the right velocity and on how repeatable the engine's shutdown transient ("tail-off" impulse) is. A high-thrust engine produces high acceleration near burnout, when the stage is nearly empty, so any timing error or variation in tail-off translates into a larger velocity error. Lower acceleration makes that error smaller, which is why many vehicles throttle down before cutoff, or shut down the main engine and finish with small vernier engines or reaction-control thrusters. Examples include the vernier engines on Atlas and Soyuz stages, and dedicated trim stages such as Minotaur's HAPS or Vega's AVUM, which clean up after solid motors that can't be shut off on command.

Plenty of upper stages achieve excellent accuracy with a single fairly high-thrust engine, such as Falcon 9's Merlin Vacuum, through precise guidance, throttling and predictable shutdown. Low-thrust engines such as Centaur's RL10 are chosen mainly for efficiency and mass; precision is a side benefit.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer:
No, a low-thrust upper-stage engine is not required to insert payloads into orbit accurately without overshooting. SpaceX’s Falcon 9 demonstrates this routinely: its Merlin Vacuum engine produces 981 kilonewtons of thrust—nearly ten times that of a traditional Centaur RL10—yet still achieves pinpoint orbital insertion comparable to low-thrust stages.

High-thrust liquid upper stages prevent overshooting through three main mechanisms. First, the engine typically throttles down near the end of the burn to cap peak acceleration and slow the rate of velocity gain as propellant mass drops. Second, modern flight computers run high-frequency navigation loops paired with fast-acting valves, commanding shutdown slightly early to compensate for the predictable "tail-off" impulse generated as residual propellants clear the chamber. Third, when sub-meter-per-second accuracy is needed—or on solid-rocket upper stages with less predictable burnouts—guidance can bias main cutoff slightly conservative and trim the final velocity using small reaction control thrusters.

In practice, upper stages often use smaller, lower-thrust engines primarily to minimize engine dry mass—every kilogram saved adds directly to payload capacity—rather than to avoid overshooting.

noweb.answer:
No, a low-thrust engine is not required for accurate orbital insertion. SpaceX’s Falcon 9, for example, uses a high-thrust Merlin Vacuum engine that accelerates its nearly empty upper stage at several g's right before cutoff while still achieving precise target orbits. Insertion accuracy depends less on low acceleration and more on fast, repeatable valve shutdowns paired with modern guidance computers that command cutoff early to account for residual thrust tail-off. Even at five g's, one millisecond of timing precision represents just five centimeters per second of velocity error, and any tiny residual error can be reduced by throttling down near burnout or trimmed afterward using small reaction-control thrusters.

Designers usually choose lower-thrust upper-stage engines not to prevent overshooting, but to maximize payload capacity. Once near orbital speed, flight is mostly horizontal and requires far less thrust to fight gravity. A smaller engine cuts upper-stage dry mass—which trades kilogram-for-kilogram with payload—and allows a larger nozzle expansion ratio within the vehicle's diameter for higher fuel efficiency.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
**No.** A low-thrust upper stage helps, but accurate insertion mainly comes from precise guidance and a precise, repeatable engine cutoff.

The error at insertion is roughly the vehicle's acceleration multiplied by the uncertainty in when the engine actually stops, plus any variation in the "tail-off" thrust as it shuts down. A stage that is still accelerating hard near burnout is less forgiving. That's why low-thrust engines like Centaur's RL10 are naturally accurate. High-thrust stages have other ways to get the same result. Falcon 9's second stage throttles its Merlin Vacuum engine down near the end of the burn. Soyuz uses small vernier engines, and Atlas once used verniers too. Some vehicles add a small trim stage or kick stage, such as Electron's Curie or the HAPS stage on Pegasus and Minotaur. Liquid engines can also be cut off on command within milliseconds, so precise shutdown timing does most of the work.

Solid motors can't be throttled or reliably cut off. They manage this by burning off excess energy with steering maneuvers, by adding a liquid trim stage, or by accepting some dispersion that the satellite's own thrusters later correct.

No, a low-thrust upper-stage engine is not required for accurate orbital insertion. While lower acceleration at engine cutoff does reduce sensitivity to timing errors—since velocity error scales with acceleration times shutdown jitter—high-thrust upper stages routinely achieve very tight orbital tolerances. For example, SpaceX's Falcon 9 uses a high-thrust Merlin Vacuum engine producing nearly one meganewton of thrust and still inserts payloads with high precision.

Launch vehicles avoid overshooting primarily through closed-loop guidance, fast and repeatable valve closures, and carefully calibrated engine shutdown transients (tail-off impulse) rather than low thrust alone. High-thrust stages can also throttle down just before cutoff, shut down engines sequentially in multi-engine designs, or use small reaction control thrusters for final trim burns.

When upper stages do use low-thrust engines, such as Centaur's RL10, the main driver is mass efficiency rather than accuracy. Once a rocket is nearly horizontal and close to orbital velocity, gravity losses are small, so using a smaller, lighter engine directly increases payload capacity.

Higher thrust does make cutoff timing more demanding. The same timing error produces a larger velocity error when the stage is accelerating faster. Low thrust is one way to improve precision, but what matters is how accurately the stage can deliver the required change in velocity.
